Hi, I would appreciate if you could help me me understand how exactly prove2.me works? I have tried to go through the website but sometimes things are a bit lost on me..

As you can see in the above discussion, we are still not able to really figure out exactly what parts to autoformalize and what parts require human led design. We collectively in physlib think that it might not be productive to have a large challenge.lean style autoformalization of statements but much more design focused autoformalizations that would help us to get to mathlib standards. So considering this it would be good to get your opinion on how to section things out for crowdsourced autoformalization. (apologies if my question is a bit vague I am still confused on how to best go about this topic :/ )
Shall we make a thread for prove2.me + physlib :)?

Hi Nathaneal this is a good question. I think it is currently best equipped to help the processes of

  • is it even possible to formalize a proof of X?
  • is it possible to formalize "intuitive" proof or proofs of X? (one approach: formalize it 100 times on the site, then choose the subgraph that is most interesting / simple to you)

I think prove2.me could be good source material to capture and evaluate AI-written formalizations of physics concepts. Then you could sift through and decide what is valuable for physlib.

Another concept is that the prove2.me directed graph really easily allows for theorem reuse. For example, we could keep a "deconstructed" version of physlib as a directed graph, and allow contributions of various quality that builds on it. Then you could look at the subgraph of prove2.me that starts with physlib content, and try to evaluate if some of it is worth adding to physlib.

I know these approaches are a little zany, but I worry that they could work well because of how quickly autoformalization is improving (see bitter lesson)

Happy to answer more questions about this.

is it possible to formalize "intuitive" proof or proofs of X? (one approach: formalize it 100 times on the site, then choose the subgraph that is most interesting / simple to you)

This is a great idea, and I think there are lots of examples in Physlib where this sort of thing would be very useful!
sorry if this was asked before, but i wanted to depend on a sorry-free version of physlib for Prove2Me. what is the best way to do this?
There should only be a few results with attribut @[sorryful] which means they depend on the Sorry axiom. Should be relatively easy to write a script which removes them.
What actually is the issue with having the sorry axiom? Is it that prove2Me would assume by default that every result used from Physlib was sorry free, without checking?

One solution is to just make Physlib sorry-free. I've done this here Physlib#1805. To quote from the description their

Historically Physlib allow sorry as long as where it appeared had the @[sorryful] attribute. One of the main reasons behind this was to allow an easy-in for people to the project. However, allowing sorry causes problems with downstream projects or projects which want to use Physlib. These include things like Prove2Me. Because informal_lemma and informal_def allow for the same sort of thing as @[sorryful], this PR removes any @[sorryful] and no longer allows sorries in Physlib.
That would be amazing! When you release a new version that is sorry-free I will have prove2me depend on it!
@Joseph Tooby-Smith any update on this?
Sorry - fell off my plate. Will work on this now, unlikely I will get it finished today, but hopefully it will be ready for another review by tomorrow
Ok, have updated this PR, and removed the awaiting-author tag so it is now back in the system
Thanks! Should I expect the next physlib release to be sorry free then? (I guess, 4.36.0 ?)
Yep! It will be! The main branch of Physlib is now sorry free to the next tagged version will be.
